passage: It was 7 pm, the office AC had switched off, and Tejas had his own client deck due by midnight. He'd already spent an hour helping the new intern, Rhea, untangle a spreadsheet, and hadn't minded; she'd been stuck, and she'd asked properly. Then Hrithik rolled his chair over. "Bro, can you just finish my summary slide? You're faster." It was the fourth time this month. Tejas remembered the Saturday he'd covered Hrithik's client call, and the cab fare Hrithik had never mentioned again. His stomach tightened; he hated saying no. He took a breath. "Not tonight, and honestly, not like this any more. I'm happy to help when you're stuck. But I've been doing your parts regularly, and it isn't working for me." Hrithik stared, then rolled back. Tejas opened his deck. His hands were a little shaky, and steady enough.

qa.q: How many times that month had Hrithik asked for help like this?
qa.a: It was the fourth time this month.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling as he took a breath before answering?
qa.a: His stomach tightened; he was nervous and hated saying no, yet he felt it had to be said 😰

qa.q: Why did Tejas's answer work better than simply saying "I'm busy"?
qa.a: He named the pattern calmly and left the door open for real need, so the limit was clear without being cruel.

qa.q: How might Rhea see Tejas, compared with how Hrithik sees him tonight?
qa.a: Rhea probably sees him as generous and patient, while Hrithik may feel suddenly cut off, even though he has received far more help.

grounding: A young professional helps an intern freely but calmly stops doing a colleague's work after a pattern of taking, despite his nerves.

passage: Gurleen's scooter keys hung by the door of her Chandigarh flat, and half the building knew it. She'd picked up Mrs Bedi's medicines from the chemist twice this week without being asked, and lent the scooter to the watchman's son for his college interview. She never kept track. Except with Nilesh from the second floor. He'd borrowed it nine times since Diwali, and it always came back on empty, once with a new scratch nobody explained. On Saturday he knocked again. "Keys, na? Just for an hour." Gurleen kept her hand on the door. "Nilesh, I'm going to stop lending you the scooter. It keeps coming back empty and you never mention it. I'm not angry. I'm just done." He laughed awkwardly. "Over petrol?" "Over the pattern," she said calmly, and closed the door gently.

qa.q: How many times had Nilesh borrowed the scooter since Diwali?
qa.a: He had borrowed it nine times since Diwali.

qa.q: What does Gurleen's "I'm not angry. I'm just done" show about her state of mind?
qa.a: She feels calm and settled rather than furious; she has decided and doesn't need a fight to hold the limit.

qa.q: What makes Gurleen's choice fair rather than stingy?
qa.a: She still helps freely with medicines and the interview, and stops only with the one person who takes without giving back, naming the reason plainly.

qa.q: Why might Nilesh laugh awkwardly and say "Over petrol?"
qa.a: Nilesh may feel caught out and embarrassed, trying to shrink the problem to petrol instead of facing the pattern she named.

grounding: A young adult who helps neighbours without counting calmly stops lending her scooter to one neighbour who habitually takes.

passage:
"Harsha, you're a lifesaver. Can I crash on your sofa again this weekend?" Gargi was already unzipping her bag.
"You stayed last weekend too."
"And the one before. But you don't mind, right?"
Harsha put the kettle on. "I didn't mind the first few times. When you lost the job, I was glad to help. I didn't want anything back."
"So...?"
"So since then it's been every weekend, and my grocery money, and you've never once asked how my week was."
Gargi stopped unzipping. "Wow. Okay."
"I'm not throwing you out tonight. Stay. But from next week, no more weekends here. If you're really stuck, tell me and we'll figure it out."
"You've been counting?"
"No. That's why it took me three months to notice."
Gargi was quiet. Then: "How was your week?"

qa.q: What did Gargi ask to do this weekend?
qa.a: Gargi asked to crash on Harsha's sofa again this weekend.

qa.q: What does Harsha's reply "That's why it took me three months to notice" reveal?
qa.a: It shows Harsha genuinely wasn't keeping score; the help was freely given, so the limit only came after a long pattern.

qa.q: Which parts of Harsha's choice kept it kind while still setting a limit?
qa.a: Harsha let Gargi stay tonight, left the door open for a real emergency, and spoke calmly about the pattern instead of blaming.

qa.q: What might be going on for Gargi when she finally asks "How was your week?"
qa.a: Gargi seems to realise, maybe with some embarrassment, that the friendship had become one-way, and tries to give something back.

grounding: A young adult who helped a friend generously calmly sets a limit once the friend keeps taking without giving back.

passage: I'm Yusuf, and I'm the friend with the camera. Over the years I've lent it to half my college batch for weddings and projects, and I've covered shoots for friends who couldn't afford a photographer. I never kept a list. It felt good. But with my cousin Shalini, something changed. She borrowed it for eight shoots in a year, all paid work for her, and it came back twice with a cracked lens cap and once with the battery dead and no charger. She never offered to share the cost. When she called last month, "Yusuf bhai, one more shoot?", for a ninth time, my chest went tight; I hate disappointing family. I took a breath and said, calmly, "Shalini, I'm not lending it for paid shoots any more. You've used it a lot and never looked after it. I'm glad to help you learn to use one, though." She was annoyed for a week. I still lend it to others.

qa.q: How many shoots did Shalini borrow the camera for in a year?
qa.a: She borrowed it for eight shoots in a year.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when Shalini called the ninth time?
qa.a: His chest went tight because he hates disappointing family, yet he knew the pattern had to stop.

qa.q: Which part of Yusuf's reply made it a fair limit rather than a punishment?
qa.a: He named the exact problem calmly and offered other help, so it was a clear limit on paid shoots, not cutting her off.

qa.q: How might Shalini see the refusal once her annoyance fades?
qa.a: She may realise she took the camera for granted and that her cousin still cares, since he offered to help her learn.

grounding: A young man lends generously without keeping score, but calmly stops lending to a cousin who habitually takes, while still helping others.

passage:
Vice-principal's note, 3 March. Written by Mrs Rao.

Sudha, twenty-five, is one of our most generous teachers. She covers classes for anyone who is ill, lends her lesson plans to new staff, and never asks for anything back. This term, though, she has covered Shreya's Class 7 periods eleven times, always at short notice, and Shreya has never once covered for her. Today I overheard Sudha in the staffroom. Shreya asked her to take Friday's periods again. Sudha said, quietly and kindly, "Shreya, I've been happy to help. But it's become every week, and it only goes one way. I can't take Friday." Shreya looked startled. Sudha went back to her marking, hands steady.

What I did next: I checked the cover register and set up a fair rota so cover is shared evenly across the staff.

qa.q: How many times had Sudha covered Shreya's periods this term?
qa.a: She had covered them eleven times.

qa.q: What does Sudha's steady hands after refusing suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she felt calm and sure about the limit, even though saying no to a colleague was not easy.

qa.q: What did Sudha get right in how she refused?
qa.a: She acknowledged she had been glad to help, named the one-way pattern plainly and kindly, and said no to Friday without blaming Shreya.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel about the new cover rota?
qa.a: Shreya might feel embarrassed at first but will know exactly what is expected, and the rest of the staff may feel the system is fairer.

grounding: A generous young teacher who helps freely calmly stops covering for a colleague who only takes, and a fair rota follows.
